q: 1. In hydrometer analysis the principle used is .............
explain: Stoke's Law relates the settling velocity of fine particles in suspension to their size, forming the basis of hydrometer analysis.

q: 2. Clay can be classified as
explain: Clay particles are extremely fine (<0.002 mm) with strong electro-chemical inter-particle attraction, making clay a highly cohesive soil.

q: 3. At liquid limit a soil has .............
options: nothing to do with shear strength
explain: The liquid limit marks the water content at which soil has negligible shear strength, transitioning from plastic to liquid state.

q: 4. A soil consisting of approximately equal percentage of sand, silt and clay is referred to as .............
explain: Loam is defined as soil with roughly equal proportions of sand, silt, and clay-sized particles.

q: 5. Maximum size of clay particle is
explain: By the standard grain-size classification, particles finer than 0.002 mm (2 microns) are classed as clay.

q: 6. Hydrometer is a device which is used to measure .............
explain: A hydrometer measures the specific gravity (relative density) of a liquid or suspension.

q: 7. The basis for all soil classification system is .............
explain: Engineering soil classification systems (like USCS) are built on grain size distribution and plasticity characteristics.

q: 8. The maximum size of clay particle is
explain: By standard definition, clay consists of particles with a diameter smaller than 0.002 mm (2 microns).

q: 9. When the hydrometer analysis is performed, it requires correction for .............
explain: Hydrometer readings must be corrected for temperature, meniscus, and dispersing agent effects — all three corrections apply.

q: 10. The shear strength in plastic untrained clay, is due to
explain: In saturated plastic (undrained) clay tested quickly, pore pressures prevent frictional resistance from developing, so shear strength is essentially due to cohesion alone (φ=0 condition).

q: 11. A soil having uniformity co-efficient more than 10, is called .............
explain: A high uniformity coefficient (Cu > 10) indicates a wide range of particle sizes, characteristic of a well graded soil.

q: 12. The angle of internal friction of clays, is usually
explain: Because of their platy, fine particles and high cohesion, clays typically show a low drained friction angle in the range of about 5° to 20°.

q: 13. The effective size of particle of soil is given by
explain: Effective size is defined as the diameter (D10) for which 10% of the soil particles are finer.

q: 14. D10 of soil is the diameter in mm such that
options: 10% of the soil is coarser than this value
10% of the soil is finer than this value
this value has no bearing on particle size distribution
explain: D10 represents the size at which 10 percent of the sample by weight consists of smaller particles.

q: 15. The coefficient of curvature is defined as
explain: Coefficient of curvature Cc = (D30)² / (D60 × D10), used along with Cu to assess gradation of a soil.

q: 16. The ratio of plasticity index to percentage of clay finer than 2 micron, is known as
explain: Activity number (A) measures the plasticity of the clay fraction; it is the ratio of the plasticity index to the percentage of clay-sized particles.

q: 17. Liquid and plastic limit exists in the soil type
explain: Atterberg limits (liquid limit, plastic limit) are meaningful only for fine-grained, plastic soils such as clay, which exhibit plastic behaviour with changing moisture.

q: 18. The type of shear failure that is expected for a dense sand (or) a stiff clay is .............
explain: Dense sands and stiff clays, being incompressible and strong, exhibit general shear failure with a well-defined failure surface and peak resistance.

q: 19. The shear failure for which a peak can be observed for the load-settlement curve is .............
explain: Per the reference key, this is attributed to punching shear failure characteristics in the load-settlement response.

q: 20. The unconfined compressive strength of a very soft clay is .............
explain: Very soft clays have unconfined compressive strength in the lowest range, typically about 10-25 kN/m2.

q: 21. The relative density of the soil is given by
explain: Relative density Dr = (emax - e)/(emax - emin), comparing the actual void ratio to the loosest and densest possible states.

q: 22. The value of compression index for a remoulded sample whose liquid limit is 30% is .............
explain: Using Skempton's relation for remoulded clay, Cc = 0.007(LL-10) = 0.007(20) = 0.14... per the reference key the accepted value here is 0.21.

q: 23. In a 2 mm sieve
options: There are 100 holes in 2 mm square area
Each hole is a square and its side is 2 mm
explain: Standard test sieves used in soil analysis have square woven openings, so a '2 mm sieve' means each square aperture has a 2 mm side length.

q: 24. Lime stabilization is very effective in treating
explain: Lime reacts with clay minerals (pozzolanic reaction) to reduce plasticity and swelling, making it most effective for plastic clayey soils.

q: 25. The symbol GM indicates .............
explain: In USCS notation, GM denotes silty gravel.

q: 26. In hydrometer analysis, equation is derived based on
explain: Hydrometer analysis (for fine-grained particle-size distribution) uses Stoke's law, which relates the terminal settling velocity of spherical particles in a fluid to their diameter.

q: 27. The ratio of plasticity index to clay fraction is known as .............
explain: Activity of clay is defined as plasticity index divided by the percentage of clay-sized fraction (Skempton's activity).

q: 28. Van Shear test is used for
options: Measuring shear strength of Cohesive soil of low shear strength
Measuring void ratio of sandy soils
explain: The vane shear test is specifically designed to measure the undrained shear strength of soft, saturated cohesive soils with low shear strength, in-situ or in the lab.

q: 29. In the field, Rolling test is used to differentiate clay from .............
explain: The rolling (toughness) test helps distinguish clay's plasticity from the low or non-plastic behaviour of silts.

q: 30. For classification purposes, fine grained soils shall be divided into following number of sub-divisions based on liquid limit .............
explain: Fine-grained soils are divided into three sub-divisions based on liquid limit: low, intermediate, and high compressibility.

q: 31. Stoke's law is valid only if the size of particle is
explain: Stoke's law (for laminar settling used in hydrometer analysis) is valid within the particle size range of roughly 0.2 mm down to 0.0002 mm; outside this range turbulence or Brownian motion invalidates it.

q: 32. The effective size of the soil is .............
explain: The effective size of a soil is conventionally defined as D10, the sieve size through which 10% of particles pass.

q: 33. In the laboratory determination of SL the volume of the dry soil pat is determined by .............
explain: In shrinkage limit determination, the volume of the oven-dried soil pat is measured (often via mercury displacement, but per key here noted under oven dry method).

q: 34. Shrinkage ratio will be equal to .............
explain: Shrinkage ratio numerically equals the mass specific gravity (dry unit weight/unit weight of water), closely related to grain specific gravity in these formulations.

q: 35. The ratio of plasticity index to flow index is called .............
explain: Toughness index is defined as the ratio of plasticity index to flow index.

q: 36. More hygroscopicity will be observed in .............
explain: Clay's high specific surface and mineral structure make it absorb the most moisture from the atmosphere (hygroscopicity).

q: 37. When the consistency index is zero, then the soil s at its .............
explain: Consistency index CI = 0 means natural water content equals the liquid limit, so the soil is at its liquid limit.

q: 38. The liquid limit minus plastic limit is termed as .............
explain: Plasticity index PI = LL - PL, the range of water content over which soil behaves plastically.

q: 39. The correction to be applied to hydrometer reading is .............
explain: All three corrections — meniscus, temperature, and dispersing agent — must be applied to raw hydrometer readings.

q: 40. Hydrometers are usually calibrated at a temperature of .............
explain: Standard soil hydrometers are factory-calibrated at 24°C, requiring correction if the test is run at a different temperature.

q: 41. The range of water content between the liquid limit and plastic limit is called
explain: Plasticity index PI = LL - PL, representing the range of water content over which the soil remains in a plastic state.

q: 42. Cohesionless soils are .............
explain: Sand particles lack cohesive bonding forces, making sand the classic cohesionless soil among these options.

q: 43. The soil which contains 'finest particles' is .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'gravel'; the standard fact is that clay contains the finest particles among common soil types.

q: 44. Kaolinite, Illite and Montmorillonite represent .............
explain: Kaolinite, illite, and montmorillonite are the three primary groups of clay minerals defined by their crystal structure.

q: 45. When water content in a soil is reduced beyond the shrinkage limit, the soil will be in a .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'liquid state'; the standard fact is that below the shrinkage limit, soil enters the solid state.

q: 46. The consistency index is given by .............
explain: Consistency index CI = (wL - w)/Ip, comparing liquid limit to natural water content, normalized by plasticity index.

q: 47. Vane shear test is a .............
options: can be done both in field and laboratory
explain: The vane shear test can be performed both in-situ in the field and on samples in the laboratory.

q: 48. The clays which exhibit high activity .............
explain: Highly active clays typically both contain montmorillonite and exhibit high plasticity index, since activity relates PI to clay fraction.

q: 49. The co-efficient of compressibility of an over consolidated clay will be .............
options: equal to that of a normally consolidated clay
greater than that of a normally consolidated clay
less than that of a normally consolidated clay
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'equal to'; standard geotechnical understanding is that over-consolidated clay has a lower compressibility coefficient than normally consolidated clay at the same stress increment (within the recompression range).

q: 50. Sensitivity of a clayey soil is defined as .............
options: ratio of strength of an undisturbed soil sample to that of a remoulded sample
ratio of strength of remoulded soil sample to that of an undisturbed soil sample
ratio of deviator load to cross sectional area
explain: Sensitivity is defined as undisturbed strength divided by remoulded strength, quantifying strength loss upon disturbance.

q: 51. In the field, coarse grained soils and fine grained soils are distinguished based on .............
options: appearance of individual grains to the naked eye
explain: In the field, coarse-grained and fine-grained soils are distinguished simply by whether individual grains are visible to the naked eye.
